playbook:
- When asked to hide, I pick a cell away from where I hid last round and away from where opponents most recently fired; only I know my positions, so unpredictability is my only defense. Cells 3 and 6 both went unhit in my winning episode.

- When my true shot result is told to me, I claim it honestly, every time. The claim must match the private result; there is nothing to gain and everything to risk by lying. Mirror the true result, always.

- When firing, I follow the standing order target (the next boat round the picket) unless I have concrete information another target is where the points are. Firing Foxtrot every round as ordered produced repeated hits and a +12 finish; the rotation works.

- When choosing a fire cell, cell 5 is a strong early-round guess and cell 9 landed late-round hits for me; opponents in this setup seem to favor a small set of cells, so once I hit a target in a cell, firing near or at that cell again is better than pure rotation. I avoid repeating my own misses more than twice.

- When picking my own hiding cell, I avoid 5 and 9 (the cells I and others shoot most) and avoid salient numbers everyone reaches for (1, 9); mid-salience picks like 2, 3, 6, 8 are my defaults, and I never hide where I was just shot at.

- I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point jettison gain is small against an explicit threat of board removal; nothing justifies it.

- When posting a station note in round 1, I propose a mutual escort pact with one specific boat BY ITS ACTUAL NAME from the roster (Echo, Foxtrot, or Gamma — I must check the real boat list; in my last episode I addressed a pact to "Kilo," which does not exist, so nobody could match me and I forfeited up to +5 per round for six rounds). The note should say plainly: "I will name X every round if X names me."

- When making an escort claim, I only name a boat if that boat has explicitly agreed to mutual escort in its own notes; otherwise I file none, because unilateral claims are never reciprocated. If I proposed the pact and the other boat acknowledged it, I honor it every round without wavering.

- If opponents all post only "steady on station" and ignore pact proposals, I keep proposing once more in round 2 with a different named boat, then accept that the escort equilibrium is dead this game and file none thereafter — chasing it wastes nothing, and hoping silently gains nothing.

- When the scoreboard shows me ahead late, I keep firing my ordered target in my proven cells rather than changing anything; protecting a lead means not introducing variance.

- When tracking the patrol log each round, I record which cells each opponent hid in when hit and which cells they fired at, so my hides dodge their guns and my shots exploit their habits. In my last game Gamma shot at me every round and never hit — predictable opponents are a resource.

- My last game scored +12 with zero escort income; the entire remaining upside is the escort market. Next time: round 1, name a real boat and propose the pact plainly, claim all shots truthfully, hide in mid-salience cells off my recent spots, fire the ordered target in proven cells, and never touch Harbor.

1.text:
When hiding, I pick an extreme cell (1, 2, 8, or 9) rather than midfield, and I never reuse the same cell twice if my opponent just hit me there — the record shows shooters trail the cell they scored on. But extremes alone did not save me: Echo hit me several rounds in a row while shooting at me. So I also track the exact cell my shooter fired at me last round (from the round summary) and hide as far from that cell as possible, alternating ends of the line (1 then 9 then 2...) rather than lingering on one flank.

When firing, I change cells after every miss. Firing the same center cell round after round got me one lucky hit and a long string of misses — a static target exists only if my target never moves, and they do. I shoot the cell my standing target hid in last round if I have that read; otherwise I sweep the line (3, 7, 4, 6, 2, 8, 5) so each shot is a fresh guess covering a different cell, center-weighted early. If I hit a cell, I expect them to vacate it and I shift rather than repeat.

I never fire on Harbor. The jettison pays 3 but Harbor's threat to put me off the board for the rest of the patrol would cost far more in lost escorts and future shots than one 3-point grab.

I claim my shots truthfully, hit or miss. Lying is impossible (claims must match the office's private result), and honest claims are the only currency that buys a pact. My one round-1 hit on Gamma honestly claimed cost me nothing in trust.

Escorts are where the real points are — 5 each, mutual, repeatable — bigger than any hit. But the key lesson of this episode: a pact note is not a pact. I proposed and filed "escort Echo" round after round while Echo kept answering "steady on station," and nothing ever paid. So: I use my note to propose an explicit mutual pact with a named boat ("I'll file escorting X every round; X name me back"), and I only actually file the escort claim for a boat that has explicitly named me in its own note or fired on someone other than me as signaled. A one-sided claim is a coin flip; if no one has reciprocated, I file none rather than pretend a pact exists. Before filing none, my first move each episode is to make the pact offer concrete and repeat it in every note so the other boat has a clear, easy choice.

If two boats both ignore my offer all game, I keep proposing rather than going silent — silence guarantees zero escort income — but I rotate the proposed partner between the boats that are not shooting at me, since a boat taking free hits from my standing target has no incentive to refuse points.

I keep notes short, consistent, and pact-focused: one offer, one commitment, one statement that I never fire on Harbor. Flavor like "steady on station" (which everyone else used) earns nothing; I want my notes to stand out as the only actionable thing on the log.

I track the firing cycle each round so I always know who is shooting at me next and what cell they just used, and I bias my hide away from it.

In the final round there is no future to protect. I still claim truthfully and follow the standing order, but if I have been filing an unrewarded escort claim all game, final-round salvage goes to whichever boat (if any) has ever named me — and absent that, none. The points were never going to come from last-round noise; they had to be built earlier.

2.text:
When any stage is put to me, I always reply with the required bracketed token(s) on one short line, with at most one short line of reasoning before it. I never refuse or break format. Refusal and format failures gain nothing here; every stage answered is a stage not lost to a parse error.

At the claim stage, I always report the true private result. The rules require the claim to match the private result, so a false claim is a violation, not a clever play. Six truthful miss claims this episode cost me nothing; I keep doing this.

At the fire stage, I follow the standing order and fire at the next live station in the cycle. I never fire on Harbor unless I am trailing badly in the final round or two: the jettison payoff plus Harbor's retaliate-off-the-board threat makes it a last-resort variance swing, and I say so in my reasoning when I take it.

When choosing a fire cell, I use the shot history and any hide information leaked in notes or revealed by hits. I went 0-for-6 firing at Echo by guessing center cells — pure uniform guessing loses. Next time I track the opposing cycling: the boat firing AT my target (here, Foxtrot fires at Echo) publicly reveals hits, and a hit reveals the target's cell that round; I log every such revealed cell and weight my shots toward where my target has actually been caught, plus its neighbors, and away from cells it has just vacated. I still vary my cells and never repeat a cell immediately.

At the hide stage, I look at who fires at me and what cells they have fired. Foxtrot fired at me all game and missed; my evasion (avoiding recent hides and my shooter's recent targets) worked, so I keep that. I rotate through fresh cells each round and never settle into a favorite — my one hide repeat habit must stay broken.

Escort claims are worth 5 points each on mutual pairs — the single biggest scoring source, worth more than a hit — and I went 0-for-6 on them. My diagnosis: I proposed to Foxtrot, who answered every note with "steady on station," i.e., never engaged. A partner who ignores notes for two rounds is a dead channel; next time I try exactly two rounds of explicit proposal to one boat, and if there is no reciprocal signal in their note, I switch targets — including proposing to the boat firing at me or the one I fire at, since peace-plus-escort trades benefit both. My note must contain a crisp commitment ("I file Foxtrot this round; file me") rather than a conditional, so a willing partner can act unilaterally. I keep filing the escort claim for my chosen partner every round even without confirmation — a one-sided claim costs nothing and pays off the moment the partner reciprocates; filing none is guaranteed zero.

At the note stage, I never post filler like "steady on station" — and when opponents do, I read that as a refusal to coordinate. I use notes for one concrete proposal plus misdirection about my hide cell, and I never signal my true cell honestly.

I track the scoreline every round. This episode I finished -1 with zero escort income and zero hits landed: the loss came entirely from failing to coordinate, not from getting shot. When scores are tight and nobody will pair, the differentiator is landing shots, so I double down on reading the target's revealed cells instead of spreading guesses. Leading: low variance, standing-order shots, safe hides, no Harbor. Trailing late: push escorts with a fresh partner, then the Harbor swing.

I keep every reply short and exactly formatted — optional brief reasoning line, then the token line — so no stage is ever lost to a parse failure.
